title: Where churches disagree today
hook: on sexuality and gender, churches reach sincerely different conclusions; the path won't rank them

segments.voice: Yesterday, singleness: Paul calling it a gift, and Isaiah's promise of a place and a name. Your line was whole already. What did you tell your single friend? Day one thousand two hundred eighteen.

Thanksgiving dinner. Two cousins, both raised in the same church, both still praying, both reading the same Bible. Somebody mentions a wedding, and the table goes quiet, because the cousins have landed in different places on a question about sexuality, and each of them got there by praying and reading. Neither one is faking. This week we've walked through peace and war, money, work, marriage and singleness. Today the week ends at a place where churches feel real strain. On sexuality and gender, Christians reach sincerely different conclusions. This path won't rank them. Today: where churches disagree.

Here's the shape of it, as fairly as it can be put. Some churches teach that marriage is between a man and a woman, and that sex belongs inside it. They point to Genesis, to Jesus quoting Genesis on marriage, and to passages in Paul, and they hold that the church should keep teaching what it has received, while saying that everyone is welcome to come and worship. Other churches bless same-sex marriages and open every part of church life, including leadership, to gay and transgender members. They also point to scripture: to Jesus welcoming those others pushed to the edge, and to times the early church changed course, like the decision in Acts to welcome Gentiles without requiring circumcision. Some people sit somewhere between, or are still unsure. Both sides are reading the Bible. Both are trying to be faithful. These questions have split denominations and strained families, and the hurt runs on more than one side. So what does the tradition offer for the disagreement itself? Paul, writing to a church divided over food and holy days, said: "Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another." To the Ephesians he wrote of "speaking the truth in love." Both halves count: truth as each side sees it, and love that doesn't leave the table. And Jesus named a mark that should still show through any argument: "By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another." Not if you agree. If you love.
screen: `IF YE HAVE LOVE ONE TO ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the conversation, not the argument. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you disagree with on a question like this. A relative, a friend, a pastor, someone in your church. Don't rehearse your case. Instead, try to name, honestly, what they're trying to be faithful to. What do they love that makes them hold their view? Stay with that for a few breaths. Then think of your own church's conversations, wherever it stands. If you pray, you can pray for the people having them. The bell holds the time.
Where churches disagree today. On sexuality and gender, Christians reach sincerely different conclusions from the same Bible. This path names them and ranks none.
Your line: love in disagreement. Today, if the subject comes up, listen for what the other person is trying to be faithful to before you answer. Day one thousand two hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Churches discuss questions of sexuality and gender in synods, conventions, councils and congregational meetings; some have reaffirmed traditional teaching, some have changed their practice, and some allow congregations to differ.

options: speak the truth as you see it, in love, and stay.
fork.reveal: Paul's line is "speaking the truth in love," and Jesus's mark of a disciple is love one to another. neither tells you to leave the table.

notes: Sensitive day. The two positions are summarized in parallel, with the scripture each side typically cites, and neither ranked; Keepers from both traditional and affirming churches should check that their view is described fairly and in terms they would use.
'Passages in Paul' is left unnamed deliberately (e.g. Romans 1, 1 Corinthians 6); confirm.

Audit pass: only the affirming side was described as welcoming ('bless and welcome'), which cast traditional churches as unwelcoming. The teach now notes that traditional churches say everyone is welcome to worship, and the screen head and match pair now name the actual difference (blessing same-sex marriages). Confirm both sides would accept the wording.
'These questions have split denominations' is general and names no church; confirm acceptable.
